notes.meaning: Naomi has a wealthy and respected relative named Boaz through her late husband Elimelech. This introduction prepares the reader for hope, showing that God had already placed someone in Bethlehem who could help Naomi and Ruth.

Ruth asks Naomi for permission to go out and glean in the fields. Under God's law in Israel, harvesters left behind dropped stalks of grain so the poor and foreigners could gather food to eat. Ruth does not wait around in self-pity, but takes the initiative to work hard for her family.

Ruth goes to the open fields and begins picking up leftover grain. To human eyes she picked a field at random, but she arrived right on the land belonging to Boaz. God was quietly guiding her ordinary choices to bring about His good plan.

Boaz arrives from Bethlehem and greets his harvesters by asking the Lord to be with them, and they bless him in return. This warm greeting shows that Boaz was a godly employer who treated his workers with dignity and faith.
Boaz notices Ruth among the gatherers and asks his field supervisor who she belongs to. In those days, a woman was usually identified by her family or household, and Boaz recognized that she was new.
The supervisor answers that she is the young woman from Moab who returned with Naomi. News of her arrival had already spread, and the foreman identifies her by her devoted choice to stay with Naomi.

The supervisor explains that Ruth politely asked permission to gather grain and has worked steadily since morning. She had only paused for a brief rest in the field shelter. Her humble request and hard work earned the supervisor's respect.

Boaz speaks directly to Ruth, calling her his daughter and telling her to stay in his fields near his young women. His fatherly tone shows genuine concern for her safety. He encourages her not to look elsewhere, promising her a secure place to gather food.

Boaz tells Ruth to keep her eyes on where his women are working and follow right behind them. He assures her that he has strictly ordered his young men not to mistreat her. He even invites her to drink from the water jars his workers filled, sparing her the hard task of drawing water herself.

Ruth bows low with her face to the ground in deep humility and gratitude. She asks why Boaz is showing such kindness to someone who is an outsider from another country. She does not feel entitled to help, but receives his grace with thankfulness.

Boaz answers that he has heard the full story of how she cared for Naomi after losing her husband. He admires how she left her parents, her home country, and everything familiar to live with a people she did not know.

Boaz asks the Lord, the God of Israel, to richly reward Ruth for what she has done. He describes her coming under God's wings for shelter, just like baby birds find warmth and safety under a mother bird. Trusting God brings true security even when we are far from home.

Ruth thanks Boaz for comforting her and speaking kindly to her heart. She notes that she does not even hold the rank of one of his servant girls, making his kindness all the more meaningful. His gentle words brought real peace to an anxious outsider.

At lunchtime, Boaz calls Ruth over to share the meal, inviting her to dip bread in sour wine sauce and handing her roasted grain. She eats until she is completely satisfied and still has food left over. Boaz treats her not like a beggar, but like an honored guest.

When Ruth gets up to work again, Boaz orders his reapers to let her gather grain directly among the tied bundles. Gleaners normally had to wait until the sheaves were carried away, so this was an extraordinary privilege.

Boaz goes even further by telling his reapers to pull stalks from the bundles on purpose and drop them for her. He commands them not to scold or embarrass her for collecting them. In this way, Boaz provides abundantly for Ruth while letting her keep her dignity as a worker.

Ruth works in the field until evening and threshes the grain with a stick right where she worked. She ends up with about an ephah of barley, which is about two-thirds of a bushel—an amazing haul for one day. Her honest labor, blessed by kindness, yielded enough grain to feed them for weeks.

Ruth carries the heavy barley back into Bethlehem to show Naomi, and gives her the food she had saved from lunch. Even while receiving generous food in the field, Ruth had remembered to provide for her mother-in-law.

Naomi is astonished by the large amount of barley and asks Ruth where she worked, blessing the man who noticed her. Ruth tells her that she worked in the field of a man named Boaz. Naomi instantly recognizes that an unseen hand was at work.

Naomi praises the Lord for continuing His steadfast love to both the living and the dead. She explains that Boaz is a close relative and one of their family redeemers—a kinsman who had the legal duty to help poor relatives and protect family land.

Ruth adds that Boaz urged her to stay with his harvest workers until the entire harvest was finished. His offer meant that Ruth and Naomi would have plenty of food and protection throughout both the barley and wheat seasons.

Naomi urges Ruth to follow Boaz's advice and stay with his young women. Working in strange fields could expose her to insults or harm, and wandering off might look like she did not appreciate Boaz's generosity.

Ruth listens to Naomi and stays close to the servant girls of Boaz until both the barley and wheat harvests end. Throughout this entire season, she remains devoted to her mother-in-law and lives with her at home.
